families.title: Card totals
families.mathematics: Two trays A and B hold number cards 0–9, and each pair a + b drops a token on a strip of totals 0–18; pairs with the same total share a token, so the strip is the sumset A + B. With m cards in A and n in B there are at least m + n − 1 and at most m × n different totals. The lower bound is a route in the addition grid (A going up, B going across) from the bottom-left dot to the top-right dot, one step right or up: each step adds, so its m + n − 1 totals are all different. When every total is on one route the design has the fewest, and with m, n ≥ 2 that happens exactly when A and B are evenly spaced with the same gap (swap the route around one square). A one-card tray only shifts the other, so any B attains the bound then. The upper bound is one token per pair, reached when no jump inside A equals a jump inside B.
rules: Each card in A pairs with each card in B. A pair drops a token on the strip at its total, and pairs with the same total share a token.
The grid shows every pair: A’s cards go up, B’s go across, and each dot holds their total.
A route starts at the bottom-left dot and steps right or up, one dot at a time, to the top-right dot.

puzzles.idea: Free play with two trays: which cards give few totals, which give many, and what a route shows.

parent.notice: Whether your child sets challenges for someone else: a number of totals, or a tray to match.
parent.prompt: Which choice of cards makes exactly 6 totals with three cards in each tray? Are there several?
parent.explanation: With m and n cards there are at least m + n − 1 and at most m × n totals, and every number in between can happen for many sizes. The fewest needs A and B evenly spaced with the same jump, unless a tray has one card.
parent.extension: Put one card in A. How many totals are there, whatever B is?
parent.connection: Sumsets, the basic objects of additive combinatorics.

puzzles.idea: Pairs land on the same total when B jumps by as much as A does; a route through the grid shows no two cards can do with fewer.
puzzles.prerequisites: Recognise 0–9; the strip does the adding, and a child who adds to 18 can check it. A grown-up can read How to play.
hints: Which pairs could land on the same total?
A jumps by 2. If B jumps by 2 too, two pairs share a total.
Put 0 and 2 in B, then walk a route through the grid.

parent.notice: Whether your child picks B at random or looks for pairs that share a total, and whether they see that the route has three dots whatever B is.
parent.prompt: Why can no B make fewer than three totals?
parent.explanation: With A = {0, 2} and B = {b, c}, b < c, the totals 0 + b, 2 + b and 2 + c are always different: they climb along the route bottom-left, up, right (or right, then up). So there are at least three totals. Three is reached exactly when 0 + c equals 2 + b, that is, when B jumps by 2: {0, 2}, {1, 3}, up to {7, 9}, eight ways.
parent.extension: In the playground, try A = {0, 3}. Which B give three totals now?
parent.connection: The smallest sumset theorem: two sets of sizes m and n have at least m + n − 1 different sums.

puzzles.provenance: Week 55 Problem 1: {0, 2} + {1, 3} gives 3 totals and {0, 2} + {1, 4} gives 4; here the child chooses B.

puzzles.objective: Choose cards for A and B that make as many different totals as you can.

puzzles.idea: All nine totals are different when B’s cards are far enough apart that none of A’s jumps fits between two of them.
puzzles.prerequisites: Recognise 0–9; the strip does the adding, and a child who adds to 18 can check it. A grown-up can read How to play.
hints: Where do two pairs land together?
A’s cards are 1, 2 and 3 apart. Two B cards that close let two pairs meet.
Put 0, 4 and 8 in B.

parent.notice: Whether your child spreads B’s cards out after seeing shaded dots, or keeps adjusting one card at a time.
parent.prompt: Why can’t there be more than nine totals?
parent.explanation: Three A cards and three B cards make nine pairs, and each pair drops one token, so nine is the most. Two pairs a + b and a′ + b′ share a total exactly when b′ − b = a − a′, a jump inside B equal to a jump inside A. A’s jumps are 1, 2 and 3, so every jump in B must be at least 4, and three such cards fit in 0–9 four ways: {0, 4, 8}, {0, 4, 9}, {0, 5, 9} and {1, 5, 9}.
parent.extension: Which B makes the fewest totals with this A? (Six, for example B = {0, 1, 3}; five would need A evenly spaced.)
parent.connection: The largest sumset: |A + B| = mn exactly when the differences of A and of B never agree (a Sidon-type condition).

puzzles.provenance: Week 55 Problem 2: the third trial {0, 1, 2} + {0, 3, 6} gives 9 totals; here A is the second trial’s {0, 1, 3}, so that only four B work, and the child chooses B.

parent.notice: Whether your child uses a route to see how many totals they must have before trying to get fewer.
parent.prompt: Could any cards make three totals?
parent.explanation: A route through a 2 × 3 grid passes 2 + 3 − 1 = 4 dots, and each step adds to the total, so every choice of cards has at least four different totals. Four is reached exactly when A and B jump by the same amount: A = {a, a + d} and B = {b, b + d, b + 2d}.
parent.extension: Predict the fewest for three and four cards, then try it in the playground.
parent.connection: The lower bound m + n − 1, proved by one monotone path in the addition table.

puzzles.provenance: Week 55 Problem 4, the 2 + 3 sizes: “choose cards that make the fewest possible different totals”.

puzzles.prerequisites: Choose several cards with a plan in mind and keep track of which pairs share a total.
hints: Which totals must be different whatever cards you choose?
A route has five dots. For every total to be on it, each step around a square of the grid must give the same total either way.
Put 0, 1 and 2 in A and the same in B, then walk a route.

parent.notice: Whether your child finds that equal jumps help, and whether they try different jumps in A and B.
parent.prompt: You have 5 totals and a route through all of them. Why can no cards make 4?
parent.explanation: Any route through a 3 × 3 grid passes 5 dots with growing totals, so every choice has at least 5 totals. If every total is on the route, swap the route around one small square: both routes must have the same totals, so the two corners of that square hold the same total, and the jump in A there equals the jump in B. That holds for every square, so A and B are evenly spaced with one gap. 120 of the 14,400 choices of three and three cards from 0–9 do it.
parent.extension: Is the fewest for four and four cards 7? Try it (puzzle 11).
parent.connection: The inverse theorem: for m, n ≥ 2, |A + B| = m + n − 1 exactly when A and B are arithmetic progressions with the same difference.

puzzles.provenance: Week 55 Problem 3, “make as few different totals as you can”, with the route certificate of Problems 8 and 9.

puzzles.title: Every B
puzzles.objective: Find every B of two cards that makes exactly 4 different totals with this A. Press That’s all when none is left.
puzzles.instruction: Find every B of two cards that makes exactly 4 different totals with this A. Press That’s all when none is left.
puzzles.controls: Tap a card to put it in B, and tap it again to take it out. Press That’s all when you are sure. Undo takes back the last card.
rules: Each card in A pairs with each card in B. A pair drops a token on the strip at its total, and pairs with the same total share a token.
The grid shows every pair: A’s cards go up, B’s go across, and each dot holds their total.
Each B that works joins the row above the strip. Press That’s all when you think none is left. It says if there is another.
puzzles.idea: The B trays that give the fewest totals are exactly the ones that jump by A’s jump.
puzzles.prerequisites: Keep the trays already found in mind and decide when none is left.
hints: Try a B: which pairs land on the same total?
Each one found has the same jump between its two cards.
Every B that jumps by 3 works: from 0 and 3 up to 6 and 9.

parent.notice: Whether your child finds B trays one by one at random or notices the jump of 3 and slides it along.
parent.prompt: How do you know there isn’t another?
parent.explanation: With B = {b, b + d}, the six pairs give A + b and A + b + d, two copies of {0, 3, 6} shifted. They overlap in two totals exactly when d = 3, A’s jump; d = 6 overlaps one total and any other jump none. So four totals means B = {t, t + 3}, and t can be 0 to 6: seven trays.
parent.extension: Which B trays give five totals? (Puzzle 10.)
parent.connection: The equality case of the sumset bound, found by a complete search.

puzzles.provenance: Week 55 Problem 5: A = {0, 3, 6}, every two-card B from 0–9 with four totals; no answer slots here.

puzzles.title: Two even trays
puzzles.objective: Choose evenly spaced cards for A and for B that make as many different totals as you can.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Both trays evenly spaced, as many totals as you can.
puzzles.instruction: Choose evenly spaced cards for A and for B that make as many different totals as you can.
puzzles.controls: Tap a card to put it in its tray, and tap it again to take it out. The dots by a tray show how many cards it holds. Undo takes back the last move.
rules: Each card in A pairs with each card in B. A pair drops a token on the strip at its total, and pairs with the same total share a token.
The grid shows every pair: A’s cards go up, B’s go across, and each dot holds their total.
Dots that share a total are shaded.
Evenly spaced means the same jump between each card and the next.
puzzles.idea: Two evenly spaced trays need the same jump to make few totals; with different jumps they can make the most.
puzzles.prerequisites: Choose several cards with a plan in mind and keep track of which pairs share a total.
hints: Do evenly spaced trays always give few totals?
Try A jumping by 2 and B jumping by 3.
Put 0, 2 and 4 in A and 0, 3 and 6 in B.

parent.notice: Whether your child expects evenly spaced trays to give few totals, as in puzzle 4.
parent.prompt: Both trays are evenly spaced. Why are all nine totals different?
parent.explanation: With A = {0, 2, 4} and B = {0, 3, 6}, two pairs share a total only when a jump in B equals a jump in A. A’s jumps are 2 and 4 and B’s are 3 and 6, so none agree and all nine totals differ. Even spacing gives the fewest only when the two gaps are the same.
parent.extension: Which pairs of jumps give nine totals? (Any two of 1, 2, 3, 4 where neither is the other or twice the other.)
parent.connection: The inverse theorem needs one common difference; two progressions with unrelated differences give a sumset as large as possible.

puzzles.provenance: Week 55 Problem 6 and the review card’s fix 5: {0, 2, 4} + {0, 3, 6}, both equally spaced, with 9 totals.

puzzles.title: Uneven B
puzzles.objective: Choose cards for A so that one route through the grid passes every total.
puzzles.instruction: Choose cards for A so that one route through the grid passes every total.
puzzles.controls: Tap a card to put it in A, and tap it again to take it out. Tap the dots of a route one at a time, starting at the bottom-left; tapping the top-right dot checks it. Tap a dot of your route to take back the taps from there. Undo takes back the last move.

The grid shows every pair: A’s cards go up, B’s go across, and each dot holds their total.
A route starts at the bottom-left dot and steps right or up, one dot at a time, to the top-right dot.
Finish by tapping a route that passes every total on the strip; the top-right dot checks it. A may have one, two or three cards; a route with one card counts once a route with more has been tried.
puzzles.idea: With an uneven B, every total fits on one route only when A has a single card: one card shifts B without merging any totals.
puzzles.prerequisites: Follow right and up steps on a grid, and see that a route’s totals keep growing.
hints: Tap a route through the grid. Which total does it miss?
B jumps by 1 and then 2. Two A cards would need to jump by both at once.
After a route with two cards is refused, take cards out of A until it has just one.

parent.notice: Whether your child keeps trying two-card A trays, and what they make of the one-card solve. A starts with two cards, and a one-card route counts only after a route with more cards has been refused, so the solve follows a real attempt.
parent.prompt: Why does one A card always work, even though B is uneven?
parent.explanation: With A = {a}, the totals are a + 0, a + 1 and a + 3: B shifted by a, three different totals, and the grid is one row, so the route passes them all. With two A cards {a, a + d} there are at least four totals but a route passes only four dots; every total fits only if d equals both of B’s jumps, 1 and 2, which is impossible. So the theorem’s “evenly spaced” needs two cards in each tray.
parent.extension: Is there a B tray of three cards for which some two-card A fits every total on one route? (Yes: any evenly spaced B, with A jumping by B’s gap.)
parent.connection: The exception in the inverse theorem: when one set is a singleton, |A + B| = |B| for every B.

puzzles.provenance: Week 55 Problem 7: {4} + {0, 1, 3} gives 3 totals, and “Does B need equal spacing?”

parent.notice: Whether your child tries B jumping by 1 or 2 first, and how they see that only a jump of 3 can work.
parent.prompt: Why is there only one B?
parent.explanation: A route through a 3 × 4 grid passes 3 + 4 − 1 = 6 dots, so there are at least six totals. Every total on one route forces A and B to share a gap (puzzle 4), and A’s gap is 3, so B = {t, t + 3, t + 6, t + 9}; within 0–9 only t = 0 fits.
parent.extension: With A = {1, 3, 5}, how many four-card B give six totals? (Four: B jumps by 2 and starts at 0, 1, 2 or 3.)
parent.connection: The inverse theorem pins B down once A is given.

puzzles.title: Many from four
puzzles.objective: Choose cards for A and B that make as many different totals as you can.
puzzles.visibleObjective: As many totals as you can.
puzzles.instruction: Choose cards for A and B that make as many different totals as you can.

puzzles.idea: Sixteen different totals from four and four cards needs every jump in A to differ from every jump in B, and 0–9 leaves very little room.
puzzles.prerequisites: Choose several cards with a plan in mind and keep track of which pairs share a total.
hints: Fill both trays and look at the shaded dots. Which pairs land together?
Two pairs share a total when a jump inside A equals a jump inside B. Give one tray small jumps and the other jumps too big for them, inside 0–9.
Put 0, 1, 8 and 9 in A and 0, 2, 4 and 6 in B.

parent.notice: Whether your child plans the jumps of each tray, or changes cards one by one after shaded dots appear.
parent.prompt: Why can’t A be four cards in a row?
parent.explanation: Two pairs share a total exactly when a jump inside A equals a jump inside B. Four cards in a row have jumps 1, 2 and 3, so B’s cards would all need to be at least 4 apart, which takes 12 in 0–9. The only way is A = {0, 1, 8, 9} (jumps 1, 7, 8 and 9) with B four cards two apart, or the same with A and B exchanged: 8 of the 44,100 choices.
parent.extension: What is the fewest for four and four? (Puzzle 11.)
parent.connection: The upper bound mn, reached when the difference sets of A and B meet only in 0.

puzzles.provenance: The Week 55 review card’s fix 4 and App fit: 4 + 4 with 16 totals, “only {0, 1, 8, 9} with four cards of gap 2”.

puzzles.title: Every B again
puzzles.objective: Find every B of two cards that makes exactly 5 different totals with this A. Press That’s all when none is left.
puzzles.instruction: Find every B of two cards that makes exactly 5 different totals with this A. Press That’s all when none is left.
puzzles.controls: Tap a card to put it in B, and tap it again to take it out. Press That’s all when you are sure. Undo takes back the last card.

puzzles.idea: The jump inside B decides how many pairs land together: a jump A makes once gives one shared total.
puzzles.prerequisites: Keep the trays already found in mind and decide when none is left.
hints: Which jumps in B make two pairs land together?
A jumps 3 twice and 6 once. A B that jumps by 3 shares two totals.
Every B that jumps by 6 works: from 0 and 6 up to 3 and 9.

parent.notice: After puzzle 5, whether your child tries jumps other than 3 and notices which one shares a single total.
parent.prompt: Why does a jump of 6 share one total and a jump of 3 share two?
parent.explanation: B = {b, b + d} gives A + b and A + b + d. A total is shared when a card of A plus d is another card of A. In {0, 3, 6}, adding 3 lands on another card twice (0 → 3, 3 → 6) and adding 6 once (0 → 6). So d = 6 gives 6 − 1 = 5 totals: B = {0, 6}, {1, 7}, {2, 8} or {3, 9}.
parent.extension: Which two-card B give six totals with this A? (Every B whose jump is not 3 or 6.)
parent.connection: The number of shared totals counts the representations of d as a difference of A, the start of additive energy.

puzzles.provenance: New, from Week 55 Problem 5’s method with a different count.

puzzles.prerequisites: Choose several cards with a plan in mind and keep track of which pairs share a total.
hints: How many dots does a route through a 4 × 4 grid pass?
Seven. For every total to be on one route, A and B must jump by the same amount everywhere.
Put 0, 1, 2 and 3 in A and the same in B, then walk a route.

parent.notice: Whether your child predicts 7 from the route before building it.
parent.prompt: Could a gap of 2 work? A gap of 3?
parent.explanation: A route passes 4 + 4 − 1 = 7 dots with growing totals, so there are at least 7. Seven means every total is on one route, which forces A and B to jump by one common gap d. Gap 1: 7 starts each, 49 ways; gap 2: 4 each, 16 ways; gap 3: only {0, 3, 6, 9}, 1 way. 66 of 44,100.
parent.extension: With a route and a square, explain to a grown-up why every gap must be the same.
parent.connection: The inverse theorem for the smallest sumset, proved by swapping the path around one square.

puzzles.provenance: The Week 55 review card’s fix 4: 4 + 4, fewest 7.
